lesson.title: Reisen I: das Fahrrad, der Koffer, die Karte, die Haltestelle, das Dorf
lesson.subtitle: wheels, luggage and the road out of town — a travel kit built from verbs and baskets you already own

hook.title: Out of Town in Five Words
hook.content: das Fahrrad is fahren + Rad — the driving-wheel, compounded out of the go-verb you have owned since early on. der Koffer is Latin cophinus, a wicker basket, that walked to German through Old French and Dutch — and to English as coffin: the box you travel with and the box nobody comes home from are the same word. die Karte is Latin charta, 'a sheet of papyrus' — German hardened the c to K and kept one word, while English split the sheet into card and chart. die Haltestelle is halten (English hold with the D→T badge, the Tag/day family) + Stelle, 'place': the place where the bus holds still. And das Dorf is Proto-Germanic *þurpą, the village: German hardened þ→d and kept the everyday word, English kept the th and lost the word — it survives only in place names like Scunthorpe and Grimethorpe, which are Dörfer that never left the map.

footnotes.title: English Took the Basket Twice
footnotes.content: Latin cophinus reached English through Old French two times over: as coffin, the funeral box (from cofin), and as coffer, the treasure chest (from cofre). German's Koffer came by the cofre route — Dutch koffer — so der Koffer is really English coffer wearing travel clothes. One Latin basket, three boxes.

pattern.title: The Travel Kit in Frames
pattern.content: Four frames. 1. Ride: Ich fahre mit dem Fahrrad (I go by bike) — mit + dem does the riding, fahren does the going. 2. Search: Ich suche den Weg auf der Karte (I look for the way on the map) — auf + der says where the search happens. 3. Stand: Die Haltestelle ist gleich hier (the stop is right here) — gleich is the 'right' of right here, the same gleich as in looking alike. 4. Arrive small: Das Dorf ist klein und alt — and if you missed it, Der Zug fährt sehr früh is the sentence that explains why.
pattern.linguist_note: The Danelaw is why England still speaks of thorpes: Old Norse þorp and Old English þorp are the same *þurpą as German Dorf. The common noun died in English, but the map kept it — Scunthorpe, Grimethorpe and their neighbors are a list of Dörfer across the old Danelaw.

exercises.prompt: Out of town — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: I am looking for the way on the map
matching_pairs.german: Ich suche den Weg auf der Karte

matching_pairs.english: The bus stop is right here
The village is small and old
matching_pairs.german: Das Dorf ist klein und alt

matching_pairs.english: The village is over there — we take a detour
matching_pairs.german: Das Dorf ist drüben, wir nehmen einen Umweg

matching_pairs.english: The church is on the left, the house on the right
matching_pairs.german: Die Kirche ist links, das Haus rechts

matching_pairs.english: The street crosses through the village
matching_pairs.german: Die Straße geht quer durch das Dorf

matching_pairs.english: Along the river is the village
matching_pairs.german: Den Fluss entlang ist das Dorf

exercises.target_answer: Ich fahre mit dem Fahrrad, Mein Koffer ist zu schwer, Ich suche den Weg auf der Karte, Die Haltestelle ist gleich hier, Das Dorf ist klein und alt, Der Zug fährt sehr früh, Das Dorf ist drüben, wir nehmen einen Umweg, Die Wohnung gegenüber ist klein, Die Kirche ist links, das Haus rechts, Die Straße geht quer durch das Dorf, Den Fluss entlang ist das Dorf
exercises.meaning: bike, suitcase, map, bus stop, village, early train
exercises.explanation: Six travel frames, no new verbs: fahre carries das Fahrrad, sucht reads die Karte, and fährt is the same fahren in the Zug. Too heavy is zu schwer — zu doubling as 'too', exactly like English.

exercises.prompt: One of today's five wears the TH→D badge — the same hardening that made drei out of three and Bruder out of brother. Which?
exercises.meaning: das Dorf ↔ thorpe: the TH→D family
exercises.explanation: Proto-Germanic *þurpą 'village': German hardened þ to d (Dorf), English kept the th (thorp, thorpe) and then lost the word. English kept it on the map — Scunthorpe is a Dorf that never left.

exercises.prompt: Greek kóphinos became Latin cophinus, 'wicker basket'. German took the traveler's box as der Koffer. English took the same basket as a box nobody comes home from. Give the English twin:
exercises.meaning: der Koffer ↔ coffin: one Latin cophinus, two boxes
exercises.explanation: coffin came through Old French cofin; German's Koffer came through Old French cofre via Dutch — the route English also used for coffer, the money chest. Same Latin basket, and the travel box and the funeral box are etymological twins.

exercises.english_hint: fahren (to go, to drive) + das Rad (the wheel)
exercises.meaning: das Fahrrad = the bicycle, the driving-wheel
exercises.explanation: das Fahrrad is fahren + Rad: the driving-wheel. German named the machine by what it does; English went Latin-Greek instead — bi-cycle, 'two wheels' (Greek kyklos, wheel).

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I go to the village by bike'
exercises.target_answer: Ich fahre mit dem Fahrrad ins Dorf
exercises.meaning: I go to the village by bike

vocab_hints.note: ins is in + das contracted — motion into a das-noun: ins Dorf, ins Haus. English does the same with 'into the'.

exercises.explanation: fahren in slot 2, mit + dem for the bike, ins for motion into the das-noun. The bank offers der Koffer and die Stadt to prove the frame scales: Ich fahre mit dem Fahrrad in die Stadt.

summary.outcome: Name the travel kit and ride, search, wait and arrive with compounds that decompose into words you own.

use_example.german: Ich fahre mit dem Fahrrad ins Dorf — der Koffer ist zu schwer.
use_example.english: I go to the village by bike — the suitcase is too heavy.

summary.takeaway: Fahrrad = fahren + Rad; Koffer is coffin's Latin cousin (cophinus); Karte is card/chart from charta; Haltestelle hides halten (hold, D→T); Dorf is thorpe with the TH→D badge.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the timetable — Fahrkarte, Fahrplan, Abfahrt, Ankunft, Flughafen, every one built from a verb you already own.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Reisen I: das Fahrrad, der Koffer, die Karte, die Haltestelle, das Dorf (I go to the village by bike):
twist.target_answer: Ich fahre mit dem Fahrrad ins Dorf
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich fahre mit dem Fahrrad ins Dorf" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Reisen I: das Fahrrad, der Koffer, die Karte, die Haltestelle, das Dorf without relying on short-term echo.

fahrrad.etymology_derivation: fahren (to drive, the fare root) + Rad (wheel): the driving-wheel. [wiktionary]

koffer.etymology_derivation: Through Middle Dutch from Old French cofre — the French loan English also took as coffer and coffin. [wiktionary]

karte.context_phrase: Ich brauche eine Karte für die U-Bahn.
karte.context_translation: I need a ticket for the underground.
karte.etymology_derivation: From Latin charta through Old French carte — the page compares English card: the same paper-word, borrowed in both languages. [wiktionary]

haltestelle.context_translation: The bus stop is right here.
haltestelle.etymology_derivation: halten (to hold) + Stelle (place, from the same old place-root as English stall): a hold-place, where the vehicle stops. [wiktionary]

dorf.context_phrase: Das Dorf liegt hinter dem Berg.
dorf.context_translation: The village lies behind the mountain.
dorf.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *thurpa — Old English thorp, which survives in English place names like Mablethorpe; the English th hardened into German d. [wiktionary]

hier.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hēr — the explicit cognate of English here. [wiktionary]

drüben.context_translation: The post office is over there.
drüben.etymology_derivation: From a rare üben, a variant of über formed by the analogy of unter/unten and ober/oben — literally over yonder; über is the twin of over. [wiktionary]

umweg.context_phrase: Wir nehmen einen Umweg wegen der Baustelle.
umweg.context_translation: We take a detour because of the construction site.
umweg.etymology_derivation: um + Weg, from Middle High German umbe, around, plus wec, way; Weg is the documented twin of way — an around-way, a detour. [wiktionary]

gegenüber.context_phrase: Der Supermarkt ist gegenüber der Bank.
gegenüber.context_translation: The supermarket is opposite the bank.
gegenüber.etymology_derivation: gegen + über — literally over-against; über is the twin of English over (both from PIE *upér) and gegen the twin of against. [wiktionary]

links.context_translation: The bank is on the left.
links.etymology_derivation: Middle High German linkes; only Dutch links is a cognate — no English cognate, memorize this one. [wiktionary]

rechts.context_translation: The car is on the right.
rechts.etymology_derivation: recht + adverbial -s; recht is the direct cognate of English right (Recht, already known). [wiktionary]

quer.context_phrase: Der Baum liegt quer über dem Weg.
quer.context_translation: The tree lies across the path.
quer.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *þwerh, oblique (Old High German twerh); etymonline lists German quer as a cognate of English thwart, from Old Norse þverr, across. [wiktionary][etymonline]

entlang.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Middle Low German entlanc, essentially in lang — the lang element is the twin of English long, so it works just like along. [wiktionary]

wohnung.context_phrase: Meine Wohnung ist im dritten Stock.
wohnung.context_translation: My apartment is on the third floor.
wohnung.etymology_derivation: Wohnen (to dwell) plus -ung; the page documents the archaic English cognate woning (dwelling-place) from the same dwelling-word. [wiktionary]

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

zug.etymology_derivation: Noun of ziehen (to pull — the tow/tug family): a train is 'the pull(er)', an elevator the Aufzug ('up-pull'). [wiktionary]

uhr.etymology_derivation: Loan-cognate of hour (Latin hōra via French), and a distant doublet of Jahr and year (PIE *yóh₁r̥). German alone turned it into the word for the clock itself. [wiktionary]

stadt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *stadiz — the twin of stead (homestead, instead); final d devoiced to [t]. [wiktionary]

fluss.context_phrase: Der Fluss fließt durch die Stadt.
fluss.context_translation: The river flows through the city.
fluss.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German vluȥ, from Proto-Germanic *flutiz, from the same root as fließen, to flow. English flow is the cognate of that root. [wiktionary]

berg.context_phrase: Der Berg ist im Winter weiß.
berg.context_translation: The mountain is white in winter.
berg.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bërg, from Proto-West Germanic *berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz. English barrow, a burial hill, is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

klein.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *klainiz 'clean, fine' — the TRUE twin of English clean; the meaning drifted from 'clean' to 'small'. [wiktionary]

alt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *aldaz — the twin of old; the l stayed, the vowel and final d/t report the shift. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
